questions.question: In UPSC REVISION: Environment & Ecology (Days 85–90), this exam clue belongs to which area: "A.G. Tansley is associated with the concept of ecosystem, meaning organisms and their physical environment functioning together as one system, Ernst Haeckel is..."?
questions.explanation: Ecology Recap: A.G. Tansley is associated with the concept of ecosystem, meaning organisms and their physical environment functioning together as one system, Ernst Haeckel is associated with ecology, the study of interactions between organisms and their environment. Lindeman's 10 percent law says only about one-tenth of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems; edge effect means species diversity is often high at that boundary. A niche is the functional role of a species, including where it lives, what it uses, and how it interacts in the ecosystem. Mutualism is a +/+ interaction where both species benefit; lichen is the standard example of algae and fungus association.

quick_notes.title: Ecology Recap
quick_notes.detail: A.G. Tansley is associated with the concept of ecosystem, meaning organisms and their physical environment functioning together as one system, Ernst Haeckel is associated with ecology, the study of interactions between organisms and their environment. Lindeman's 10 percent law says only about one-tenth of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems; edge effect means species diversity is often high at that boundary. A niche is the functional role of a species, including where it lives, what it uses, and how it interacts in the ecosystem. Mutualism is a +/+ interaction where both species benefit; lichen is the standard example of algae and fungus association.
quick_notes.explanation: Ecology is the study of how living things interact with each other and with their non-living surroundings; the word was first used by a scientist named Ernst Haeckel. Later, another scientist named A.G. Tansley introduced the idea of an ecosystem, which means a community of organisms together with the physical environment (like air, water, soil) functioning as a single unit. Inside an ecosystem, energy moves through different feeding levels called trophic levels, and Raymond Lindeman's ten percent law explains that only about 10 percent of the energy from one trophic level gets passed to the next level. An ecotone is a transition zone where two different ecosystems meet, such as where a forest meets a grassland, and the edge effect describes how that boundary often has more species diversity than either ecosystem alone. A niche is the specific role and position a species has in its environment, including where it lives, what it eats, and how it interacts with other organisms. Mutualism is a type of interaction where both species benefit, and a common textbook example is a lichen, which is a partnership between an alga and a fungus.

quick_notes.title: Biodiversity Recap
quick_notes.detail: India has four biodiversity hotspots: Himalaya, Western Ghats, Indo-Burma, and Sundaland/Nicobar region. In-situ conservation protects species inside their natural habitat, such as National Parks and Biosphere Reserves, whereas Ex-situ conservation protects species outside natural habitat, such as zoos, botanical gardens, gene banks, and seed banks. IUCN Red List categories include Critically Endangered and Endangered; Great Indian Bustard is commonly cited as Critically Endangered and tiger as Endangered.
quick_notes.explanation: Biodiversity hotspots are regions that have a very high number of unique species found nowhere else and are also under serious threat from human activities. India has four such hotspots: the Himalaya, the Western Ghats, the Indo-Burma region, and the Sundaland region which includes the Nicobar islands. Conservation methods are divided into two types: in-situ conservation protects species inside their natural habitat, for example by creating National Parks (protected areas for wildlife) and Biosphere Reserves (large areas that combine conservation with sustainable use), while ex-situ conservation protects species outside their natural habitat, such as in zoos, botanical gardens, gene banks, and seed banks. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) maintains a Red List that classifies species by their risk of extinction; two important categories are Critically Endangered (facing an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild) and Endangered (facing a very high risk). For example, the Great Indian Bustard is classified as Critically Endangered, and the tiger is classified as Endangered.

quick_notes.title: Treaties Recap
quick_notes.detail: UNFCCC came from the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and is the framework convention for climate change negotiations. Kyoto Protocol set binding greenhouse gas emission reduction targets mainly for developed countries. Paris Agreement uses Nationally Determined Contributions, where countries submit their own climate action targets. Montreal Protocol protects the ozone layer; Kigali Amendment targets phasedown of HFCs. Convention on Biological Diversity is linked with Nagoya Protocol on benefit sharing and Cartagena Protocol on biosafety.
quick_notes.explanation: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, or UNFCCC, was created at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and is the main international agreement that sets up the rules for countries to negotiate how to deal with climate change. The Kyoto Protocol was a treaty under the UNFCCC that set specific, legally binding targets to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, which are gases that trap heat in the atmosphere, but these targets applied mainly to developed, wealthier countries. The Paris Agreement, also under the UNFCCC, replaced the Kyoto Protocol and uses a system called Nationally Determined Contributions, or NDCs, where each country decides and submits its own voluntary plan to cut emissions and adapt to climate change. The Montreal Protocol is a separate treaty designed to protect the ozone layer, which is a part of the atmosphere that shields us from harmful ultraviolet radiation, by banning substances that destroy it, and the Kigali Amendment to this treaty specifically targets the phasedown of hydrofluorocarbons, or HFCs, which are powerful greenhouse gases used in cooling systems. The Convention on Biological Diversity, or CBD, is a treaty focused on protecting all forms of life on Earth, and it is linked to the Nagoya Protocol, which sets rules for sharing the benefits from using genetic resources, and the Cartagena Protocol, which ensures the safe handling and transport of genetically modified organisms.

quick_notes.title: Indian Laws Recap
quick_notes.detail: Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 protects wild animals, birds, and plants through schedules of protection. Environment Protection Act, 1986 is an umbrella law giving the Union government broad powers to protect the environment. National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 created a specialized tribunal for environmental cases. Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognizes forest rights and gives Gram Sabha an important role in claims and community forest resource protection.
quick_notes.explanation: The Wildlife Protection Act of 1972 is a law that creates different lists, called schedules, to give different levels of protection to wild animals, birds, and plants, making it illegal to hunt or harm the species listed in the highest protection schedules. The Environment Protection Act of 1986 is a broad or umbrella law that gives the central Union government of India wide powers to take any action needed to protect and improve the environment, such as setting standards for pollution. The National Green Tribunal Act of 2010 set up a special court, called the National Green Tribunal or NGT, which is a specialized tribunal that only hears and decides cases related to environmental issues like pollution or forest damage. The Forest Rights Act of 2006, whose full name is the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, officially recognizes the legal rights of forest-dwelling communities to live in and use the forest. Under this Act, the Gram Sabha, which is the general assembly of all adult voters in a village, has the important power to receive and decide on claims for these forest rights and to help protect the community forest resources.

quick_notes.title: Species & Pollutants
quick_notes.detail: High Biological Oxygen Demand indicates organic pollution because microbes consume more dissolved oxygen. Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of water bodies leading to algal bloom and oxygen depletion. Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of persistent toxins at higher trophic levels. Fly ash is a major particulate waste from coal-based thermal power plants.
quick_notes.explanation: High Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) means that a lot of oxygen is being used up by tiny living things called microbes as they break down organic waste in water, so high BOD is a sign of organic pollution. Eutrophication happens when too many nutrients, like from fertilisers or sewage, enter a lake or river, causing a thick growth of algae called an algal bloom; when the algae die, their decay uses up the water's oxygen, killing fish. Biomagnification is the process where a harmful chemical, such as a pesticide, becomes more and more concentrated as it moves up the food chain, so top predators like eagles or humans get the highest, most dangerous amounts. Fly ash is a fine, powdery waste that comes from burning coal in thermal power plants, and it can pollute the air and water if not properly controlled.
